entries.title: Unique healthcare ML challenges
entries.explanation: Errors affect lives, making robustness, fairness, and accountability essential. Disease subtyping is unsupervised, while treatment questions often require causal inference. Limited labels, rare diseases, small samples, missing data, irregular intervals, and censored labels are common challenges.

entries.title: Skin cancer external validation

entries.title: Time scales; diagnosis, prognosis, therapy
entries.explanation: Cure commonly refers to acute illness, and manage to chronic illness; prevention and prediction are additional goals. Diagnosis identifies disease from signs/symptoms; prognosis concerns expected course/recovery; therapy is treatment.

entries.title: Medical cycle and diagnostic cognition
entries.explanation: Examine → data → interpret → information → determine diagnosis/prognosis → plan → therapy → examine. Generate hypotheses from the initial complaint and repeatedly activate/reject them using history and evidence. Unexpected findings prompt differential diagnosis, resembling the scientific method.

Death certificates record direct and indirect causes of death.

entries.title: Privacy–utility table
entries.explanation: Pseudonymization replaces identifiers with codes/keys and permits re-identification with the key. De-identification removes direct identifiers but may leave linkable quasi-identifiers. K-anonymity, l-diversity, and t-closeness add group constraints. Full anonymization reduces utility; differential privacy adds mathematical noise to queries/results.
entries.sourceContext: Lecture 4 — Classification Problems in Healthcare
entries.rawText: Lec 4 | Slide 3 | lec_4_classification.pdf • Privacy–utility table • Pseudonymization 用 code/key 替代标识符，有 key 可重新识别；de-identification 去 direct identifiers，quasi-identifiers 仍可能外部链接；k-anonymity、l-diversity、t-closeness 逐步约束群体；full anonymization 降低 utility；differential privacy 向结果/查询加数学噪声。 • Pseudonymization; De-identification; Quasi-identifiers; K-anonymity; L-diversity; T-closeness; Anonymization; Differential privacy

entries.title: Financial incentives; learning-system bottlenecks
entries.explanation: Affordability, quality incentives, and scarce-resource management contrast with fee-for-service overuse, fixed-budget underuse, and insurance constraints. Learning-system bottlenecks are performance→data (integration/cleaning), data→knowledge (statistics/validation/ethics), and knowledge→performance (behavioral/organizational change).

entries.title: Generalization, bias and variance
entries.explanation: Generalization is performance on new test data. Bias comes from incorrect simplifying assumptions; variance is how the fitted model changes with the training set. Underfitting: high bias/low variance and high train/test error. Overfitting: low bias/high variance, low training error, and high test error.
entries.sourceContext: Lecture 4 — Classification Problems in Healthcare

entries.title: Complexity and learning-curve diagrams
entries.explanation: As complexity increases, training error falls and test error first falls then rises. More samples reduce test error and permit greater complexity. For a fixed model, test error declines with sample size and then levels off.
entries.sourceContext: Lecture 4 — Classification Problems in Healthcare

entries.title: Error sources and cross-validation
entries.explanation: Inherent error is unavoidable; bias reflects oversimplification; variance reflects unstable estimates from limited data. Reduce variance through simpler models, cross-validation, or more data. The figure reserves a test set, then repeats actual-training/validation splits k times.
entries.sourceContext: Lecture 4 — Classification Problems in Healthcare
entries.rawText: Lec 4 | Slide 29–31 | lec_4_classification.pdf • Error sources and cross-validation • Inherent error 不可避免；bias 因过度简化；variance 因有限数据估计不稳。减 variance：简化模型、cross-validate、更多数据。图先留 test set，再反复 split actual training / validation，标 k times。 • Inherent error; Variance; Cross-validation; Training set; Validation set; Test set

entries.title: Multiclass confusion; macro vs micro
entries.explanation: For class k, the diagonal cell is TP, other cells in its actual row are FN, other cells in its predicted column are FP, and the remaining cells are TN. entries.title: Model choice and multimodal disagreement
entries.explanation: Deep learning benefits from large datasets but may be overused. Modality weights depend on context, historical reliability, and task relevance; conflicts may warrant uncertainty. entries.title: PCA data, SNR and redundancy
entries.explanation: X contains m sensors × n measurements, with each sensor centered to mean zero. High-variance directions are assumed to be signal and low-variance orthogonal directions noise; PCA seeks high SNR and less coordinate correlation. The slide's rho is an average product without division by both standard deviations; see the ambiguity note.

entries.title: Choosing PCs and dimension reduction

entries.title: PCA vs ICA and applications
entries.explanation: Both are linear transforms. PCA components are uncorrelated, orthogonal, and variance-ranked. ICA components are independent, may be nonorthogonal, and lack the same importance ordering. CT/EEG figures illustrate applications including EEG/ECG artifact removal, microarray source separation, and CT/MRI segmentation. The slides call PCA first order; retain that wording with a terminology caveat.

entries.title: PCA limitations and clinical importance
entries.explanation: PET components explaining 9%, 8%, and 4% of variance may still be clinically useful. Check before discarding and use clinically guided retention. Limits include linearity, outliers, lost interpretability, and mismatch between variance and importance.

entries.title: t-SNE affinities and objective
entries.explanation: High- and low-dimensional pairwise affinities each sum to one. KL divergence strongly penalizes moving neighbors far apart. High-dimensional Gaussians use adaptive σ_i to meet perplexity, with a lecture default of 30, followed by symmetrization. Low-dimensional affinities use a Student-t kernel, 1/(1+d²).

entries.title: DBSCAN mechanics

Core points are dense centers; border points are insufficiently dense but near a core; noise points are neither. The diagram uses Eps=1 and MinPts=5 and shows arbitrary shapes and noise. Slide 30's more-than wording differs from slide 29's minimum wording.

entries.title: DBSCAN limitations; tractography
entries.explanation: DBSCAN does not require k, handles outliers, and accommodates varied shapes/sizes. Varying densities are difficult, Eps/MinPts are hard to tune in high dimensions, and no dendrogram is produced. The MR-tractography image illustrates fiber-bundle clustering without an accuracy figure.

entries.title: Choosing cluster count
entries.explanation: Elbow: find a bend in the sum of within-cluster variances as k changes. Cross-validation: fit on m−1 parts, sum held-out squared distances to the nearest centroid, repeat m times, and compare k values.
entries.sourceContext: Lecture 6 — Unsupervised Learning in Healthcare II

entries.title: Extrinsic clustering evaluation
entries.explanation: Extrinsic evaluation uses ground truth; intrinsic evaluation uses compactness/separation without labels. Homogeneity means one true class per cluster; completeness means one cluster per true class. V-measure combines them harmonically with weighting; the slides state β∈[0,1].

entries.title: Silhouette coefficient
entries.explanation: a is mean within-cluster distance; b is the smallest mean distance to another cluster. The slides give s=(b−a)/b and say typically 0–1, with larger values better. This simplified form applies when b≥a; it is negative when a>b and does not establish a general range of only 0–1.
entries.sourceContext: Lecture 6 — Unsupervised Learning in Healthcare II
entries.rawText: Lec 6 | Slide 39 | lec_6_unsupervised_learning_II.pdf • Silhouette coefficient • a=本簇平均距离；b=其他各簇平均距离的最小值；课件式 s=(b-a)/b，称 typically 0–1、越近 1 越好。此为 b≥a 时的简式，a>b 会为负；不可据此断言一般范围仅 0–1。 • Silhouette coefficient; Intrinsic evaluation

entries.title: Cluster validation and leakage
entries.explanation: The elbow method is common. Cross-validation on unseen data is more robust but requires costly repeated clustering. Clustering all Zeisel data and then evaluating with a random forest mainly measures cluster stability, not generalization to new data.

entries.title: Potential outcomes; CATE and ATE
entries.explanation: Y0 is the control outcome and Y1 the treated outcome. CATE(x)=E[Y1−Y0 given X=x]; ATE=E[Y1−Y0]=E_X[CATE(X)]. Only one factual outcome is observed per person, leaving the other counterfactual unobserved: the fundamental problem of causal inference.

entries.title: Ignorability / no unmeasured confounders
entries.explanation: Conditional on X, (Y0,Y1) is independent of T, making groups comparable. Omitting hidden diabetes status h that affects both treatment and outcome violates this assumption.
entries.sourceContext: Lecture 8 — Causal Inference in Healthcare
entries.rawText: Lec 8 | Slide 32–36 | lec_8_causal_inference.pdf • Ignorability / no unmeasured confounders • 给定 X 后，(Y0,Y1) 与 T 条件独立；不同组可比。若隐藏 diabetes status h 同时影响 treatment 和 outcome，忽略 h 违反该假设。 • Ignorability; Unconfoundedness; Conditional independence; Unmeasured confounding; Covariates

entries.title: Common support and causal workflow
entries.explanation: Each treatment must have nonzero probability at each x: p(T=t given X=x)>0. For binary T, 0<p(T=1 given X=x)<1. Define the causal question and X/T/Y, then inspect assumptions; equal treatment-group sizes are not required.
entries.sourceContext: Lecture 8 — Causal Inference in Healthcare
entries.rawText: Lec 8 | Slide 37–38 | lec_8_causal_inference.pdf • Common support and causal workflow • 各 x 的每个 treatment 都需非零概率 p(T=t given X=x)>0；二元 T 要 0<p(T=1 given X=x)<1。先明确因果问题、X/T/Y，再审查 assumptions；不是要求两组人数相等。 • Common support; Overlap; Positivity; Causal inference

entries.title: Identification of ATE
entries.explanation: Apply iterated expectation and ignorability: E[Y1]=E_X E[Y1 given X,T=1], similarly for Y0. ATE averages the difference between factual conditional means over the population X distribution. Factual conditional distributions are learnable; counterfactual identification requires assumptions.
entries.sourceContext: Lecture 8 — Causal Inference in Healthcare
entries.rawText: Lec 8 | Slide 40–42 | lec_8_causal_inference.pdf • Identification of ATE • Iterated expectation 后用 ignorability：E[Y1]=E_X E[Y1 given X,T=1]，Y0 同理。ATE 是两个 factual conditional means 之差对总体 X 的平均；直接可学 factual 条件分布，反事实识别需假设。 • ATE identification; Iterated expectation; Ignorability; Covariate adjustment

entries.title: Response surface modeling / parametric g-formula
entries.explanation: Fit f(x,t)≈E[Y_t given T=t,X=x], predict f(x,1) and f(x,0) for each x, then average their difference to estimate ATE. The model fits factual data and fills in counterfactuals, relying on assumptions and model specification.

entries.title: Poor overlap and extrapolation
entries.explanation: When treatment groups occupy separate age ranges, equally good observed fits may imply different curves in unobserved regions and different ATEs. Extrapolation alone does not resolve missing support.
entries.sourceContext: Lecture 8 — Causal Inference in Healthcare
entries.rawText: Lec 8 | Slide 49–50 | lec_8_causal_inference.pdf • Poor overlap and extrapolation • 两治疗组年龄范围分离时，相同 observed fit 可对应不同未观察区曲线，因而不同 ATE；缺 support 不能仅靠曲线外推解决。 • Common support; Overlap; Extrapolation; Model misspecification

entries.title: RCT vs observational causal inference
entries.explanation: RCTs are the gold standard. Observational inference is useful for harmful interventions, long-term outcomes, inexpensive existing data, and broader populations, including comparative effectiveness and groups excluded from trials. It does not automatically replace RCTs.
entries.sourceContext: Lecture 9 — PyTorch Tutorial
entries.rawText: Lec 9 | Slide 3–4 | lec_9_pytorch.pdf • RCT vs observational causal inference • RCT 是 gold standard；观察性推断对有害干预、长期结局、低成本现成数据、更广人群有用，可研究 comparative effectiveness 与试验未纳入群体；不能自动代替 RCT。 • Randomized controlled trial; Observational study; Comparative effectiveness; Causal inference

entries.title: G-formula limitations
entries.explanation: Model misspecification can cause bias that more data do not automatically remove. Poor overlap makes estimates highly dependent on functional form. The slides recommend train/test fit checks; additionally, good factual fit cannot validate unobserved counterfactuals.
entries.sourceContext: Lecture 9 — PyTorch Tutorial
entries.rawText: Lec 9 | Slide 5 | lec_9_pytorch.pdf • G-formula limitations • 模型 misspecification 会产生 bias，更多数据不自动修复；poor overlap 下估计高度依赖 functional form。课件建议 train/test fit 检查；补充解释：factual fit 好仍不能验证未观察的 counterfactual。 • Parametric g-formula; Model misspecification; Bias; Common support; Extrapolation

entries.title: Convolution definition and filtering
entries.explanation: Convolution takes a weighted sum over a local neighborhood while sliding the same kernel/filter/mask across locations. Sobel detects edges and smoothing reduces variation. Slide 11's printed g(τ−x)/g[k−x] signs appear inconsistent with its flip explanation; see Part 5.

entries.title: Semantic segmentation and encoder–decoder

entries.title: Transposed convolution
entries.explanation: Upsampling adds contributions in overlapping regions. For input [[0,1],[2,3]] and the same-valued kernel, stride 1 gives [[0,0,1],[0,4,6],[4,12,9]], while stride 2 gives a 4×4 output. This does not guarantee inversion of ordinary convolution.

entries.title: Pooling, padding, CNN–RNN review
entries.explanation: Max pooling retains strong activations but may discard subtle or heterogeneous features. Same padding preserves the example's spatial size. A CNN extracts morphology and an RNN/LSTM then extracts temporal patterns. The source conflates same with zero padding; the former is a size goal and the latter a fill value.

entries.title: Architecture and sample-size heuristics
entries.explanation: Lecture heuristics: roughly 5–10 convolution layers for large classification tasks, 10–20 plus skips for segmentation, and 3–5 for small datasets; often double channels when halving spatial size. Over 10K samples may support training from scratch, 1–10K pretrained fine-tuning, and under 1K transfer/custom models. Examples include U-Net, auto-configured nnU-Net, Attention U-Net for small lesions, ResNet18/34, DenseNet feature reuse, and EfficientNet.

entries.title: Why interpret ML?
entries.explanation: Interpretability means understanding decision reasons or consistently predicting model behavior. Uses include debugging wrong features/edge cases, auditing safety/fairness/objective rules, and discovering contributions/structure/sensitivity. These matter for high-risk medical interventions, equity, and knowledge discovery.

entries.title: Intrinsic / post-hoc; local / global
entries.explanation: Intrinsic models are transparent themselves; post-hoc methods explain trained models externally, possibly one prediction at a time. Local concerns an individual, global the overall behavior. BMI<30 is only an illustration. The simple stroke-score diagram ranges from 1.9% risk at score 0 to 18.2% at score 6.

entries.title: Intrinsically interpretable models
entries.explanation: Linear/logistic regression, GLMs, decision trees, and kNN. Simple models are understandable but may struggle with complex interactions. In the PSA radiotherapy example, ridge coefficients shrink gradually while lasso can set them to zero; λ controls strength. The heart-disease tree branches on Ca, MaxHR, chest pain, and other features.

entries.title: LIME
entries.explanation: Locally Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations: sample perturbations, obtain black-box predictions, weight by proximity to the target, and fit a simple local linear surrogate. Local fidelity does not imply a global fit. Brain-imaging examples show white/gray-matter LIME values and predictor rankings.

entries.title: SHAP and coalition attribution
entries.explanation: Shapley-inspired allocation of marginal contributions: features are players and prediction/loss is profit. Alice alone earns 20, Bob 10, together 50, and the empty coalition 0. Across two orders, Alice contributes 20/40, averaging 30; Bob contributes 30/10, averaging 20. Retain the source spelling Shapely as a search alias.

entries.title: Counterfactual explanations
entries.explanation: Ask how features must change to alter a prediction. The illustration changes predicted stroke risk from 90% to 10% when BMI becomes 25, minimizing d(x,x′) subject to f(x′)=c′. This is a model counterfactual, not automatic proof of an intervention effect. The fMRI example uses GAN image-to-image conversion from MOTOR activation to an EMOTION classification.
entries.sourceContext: Lecture 11 — Interpreting ML Models in Healthcare
entries.rawText: Lec 11 | Slide 38–40 | lec_11_explaining_ML_models.pdf • Counterfactual explanations • 问如何改变 features 才改变 prediction。示意 stroke risk90%，BMI→25 后模型风险10%；优化最小 d(x,x′) 且 f(x′)=c′。这是模型反事实解释，不自动证明真实干预效应。fMRI 图用 GAN image-to-image 把 MOTOR activation 改为 EMOTION 分类。 • Counterfactual explanation; Adversarial counterfactual; Stroke; BMI; fMRI; GAN; Causal inference

entries.title: Open discussion: explanation evaluation
entries.explanation: The slides ask why healthcare needs counterfactuals, when interpretability is unnecessary, and how to compare explanations, without a standard answer or universal metric. Connect these questions to debugging, auditing, and discovery, but do not present an inferred answer as a supplied lecture answer.

entries.explanation:
$\mathcal L=\sum_{i,j}p_{ij}\log\frac{p_{ij}}{q_{ij}}$

The figure's numerator is $\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)$; both denominator factors are printed as $\sqrt{\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2}$.

**Apparent typo:** both factors use y. Standard normalization uses squared deviations for x and y separately; the printed expression is not silently corrected here.

entries.title: Sensitivity vs Specificity
entries.explanation:
**Sensitivity:** detection among actual positives; protects against missed diagnoses.

**Specificity:** correct exclusion among actual negatives; protects against false alarms.

entries.title: Factual predictive fit vs Counterfactual validity
keywords: Factual predictive fit vs Counterfactual validity
entries.explanation:
**Factual fit:** accurate predictions in the observed treatment groups.

**Counterfactual validity:** still requires confounding/overlap assumptions and valid extrapolation; good fit does not prove all assumptions.

entries.title: Ordinary vs Transposed convolution

**Convolution:** local weighted sums extract features and often reduce spatial size.

**Transposed convolution:** upsamples by summing overlapping contributions; it is not guaranteed to invert convolution.
entries.rawText: Ordinary vs Transposed convolution • Convolution • 邻域乘加提特征，常缩小空间 • Transposed convolution • 上采样，贡献重叠求和；不是保证可逆 • Lec 10 | Slide 20–23, 40–42 | lec_10_cnns_for_medical_imaging.pdf

slideEntries.explanation:

What makes healthcare different?
• Life or death decisions
• Need robust algorithms
• Checks and balances built into ML deployment
(Also arises in other applications such as autonomous driving.)
• Need for fairness and accountability
• Many questions are about unsupervised learning
• Discovering disease subtypes.
• Many of the questions we want to answer are causal.
• Naïve use of supervised machine learning is insufficient.

slideEntries.title: Health AI Deployment Experiences
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Health AI Deployment Experiences
• Epic’s sepsis model was implemented in hundreds of hospitals to
monitor patients and send an alert if they were at high risk for sepsis.
• The model uses a combination of real-time emergency room
monitoring data (heart rate, blood pressure, etc.), demographic
information, and information from the patient’s medical records.
• An external validation by the U of Michigan resulted in very poor
performance (AUC 0.63 vs the advertised AUCs of 0.73 and 0.83) 1 .
• Out of 2,552 patients with sepsis, it only identified 33% of them and
raised a lot of false alarms in the process.
Fall 2026 Varatharajah, CSCI 5526 37
1 https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/article-abstract/2781307

slideEntries.title: Student Questions
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Student Questions
I read about an article once on EPIC's failure on creating an AI model that
predicted a no-show patient. The authors evaluated the AI model and found
that the model's training data accounted for the race or the individuals
immigration status. I think it is also important to mention that a model just does
not fail because of accuracy but it can also fail because of how biased that
model is.
-- You are absolutely right. The "No-Show" model was designed to predict which
patients would skip appointments so clinics could overbook slots or target those
patients with reminders.
-- However, the model relied heavily on demographic data points, including race,
ethnicity, socioeconomic markers, and even immigration or documentation status.
-- This is an instance of algorithmic bias.
Fall 2026 Varatharajah, CSCI 5526 3

slideEntries.title: Student Questions
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Student Questions
What validations and tests would be performed in order to be approved by the
FDA?
Technical & Analytical Validation -- developers must prove the underlying machine
learning model is stable, reproducible, and precise.
Clinical Validation & Utility Testing -- AI system functions accurately and safely
when interacting with real-world clinical data.
Human Factors & Usability Engineering
Software Assurance, Lifecycle, & Cybersecurity -- AI systems must meet rigid digital
infrastructure security requirements to protect patient data and system integrity.
I know LLM systems like OpenEvidence are popular among physicians. Do these
models require FDA approval?
Under current guidance and the Cures Act, software that merely surfaces medical
literature, provides reference information, or acts as general educational literature
retrieval does not always require active FDA pre-market review.
Fall 2026 Varatharajah, CSCI 5526 4

slideEntries.title: Student Questions
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Student Questions
Many of the deployment failures discussed today were identified by comparing
predictions with ground-truth labels, for example through changes in AUC.
However, you also mentioned that many healthcare problems are unsupervised,
such as discovering disease subtypes. If there is no ground-truth label, how can
we detect whether an unsupervised model has failed after deployment or
whether the data distribution has changed in a clinically meaningful way? Is
comparing the distribution of X or learned representations enough, or do we still
need external outcomes or expert validation?
-- We can have measures like reconstruction error, etc to monitor unsupervised
methods.
-- But we still need expert validation.
We focused on deployed models that tried to help clinicians and nurses make
decisions regarding diagnosis and treatment planning. Have prognosis models
faced similar issues, and seen comparable successes?
-- Yes, they have faced the exact same structural failures and bias traps as
diagnostic models.

Cognitive Theory of Diagnosis
• From initial complaints, guess suitable hypothesis
• Use current active hypotheses to guide questioning
• Failure to satisfy expectations is the strongest clue to a better
hypothesis; differential diagnosis
• Hypotheses are activated, de-activated, confirmed or rejected based
on
• logical criteria
• probabilities based on:
• findings local to hypothesis
• causal relations to other hypotheses (coherence)

clinical cognition. Taking a present illness by computer. The American Journal of Medicine, 60(7),

slideEntries.title: How Does the Health System Learn?
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
How Does the Health System Learn?
• “Evidence-based medicine”
• Contrast with “Tradition-based medicine” — Apprenticeship
• Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial (RCT)
• E.g., is drug A more effective than drug B for condition X?
• Narrow selection of patient cases and controls
• Careful collection of systematically organized data
• Statistical analysis of outcomes
=> Statistically significant conclusions
• But:
• Heterogeneity: most cases to which RCT results are applied do
not fit trial criteria.
• Short follow-Up: trials run for limited times, but use is longer.
• Small samples: some effects are rare but devastating.

slideEntries.title: The Learning Healthcare System
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
The Learning Healthcare System
“One in which progress in science, informatics, and care culture align to generate new
knowledge as an ongoing, natural by-product of the care experience, and seamlessly
refine and deliver best practices for continuous improvement in health and health care”
• Needs:
• Comprehensive collation of all clinical, social, demographic, behavioral data
• Routine capture of novel data sources:
• genomes, gene expression, etc.
• environmental factors (e.g., metagenomics)
• physiological response to life situations
• Technical infrastructure
• Storage and analysis of truly “big data”
• Incentives and demonstrations of utility
• Check out the Center for Learning Health System Sciences at UMN
• https://med.umn.edu/clhss

Tracking Disease Prevalence by
Systematic Classification
• 17th century: John Graunt on the
London Bills of Mortality estimated
mortality before age 6 at 36%
• 18th century: Sauvage, Linnaeus, Cullen
made first attempts at systemic
classification
• 1853—first International Statistical
Congress led to Wm. Farr ’s system:
• epidemic diseases

• local diseases arranged according to anatomical site
• developmental diseases
• diseases that are the direct result of violence

titles, abstracted to 99, and 44
• 1920 International List of Causes of
Death
• 1920s-40s—Manual of the International
Statistical Classification of Diseases,
Injuries, and Causes of Death
• 1975—ICD-9
• 2015—ICD-10
• ICD-n are under control of the World
Health Organization (WHO)
• ICD-9CM, ICD-10CM are US “Clinical
Modifications”, mainly to support billing

slideEntries.title: Student Questions
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Student Questions
In practice, do doctors also consider financial factors? Would these factors influence how
doctors make judgments, positively or negatively?
Positives:
1. Over 60% of physicians report routinely weighing affordability when prescribing drugs or
ordering tests.
2. Financial models that reward quality and efficiency over sheer volume incentivize
doctors to focus on preventive care
3. Awareness of macro-level healthcare costs forces doctors to treat scarce resources (like
ICU beds or expensive MRI scans) with greater care.
Negatives:
1. In traditional fee-for-service payment systems, doctors or hospital groups earn more
money when they do more procedures.
2. Conversely, in fixed-budget systems (like certain HMOs or capitated insurance plans), a
clinic or hospital loses money if they order too many expensive services.
3. Doctors are often constrained by what insurance policies will approve.

slideEntries.title: Student Questions
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Student Questions
Do you think the learning healthcare system framework sometimes takes too
much time per cycle to adapt to new discoveries?
Yes.
1. The "Performance-to-Data" Bottleneck: Aggregating clean, normalized data
across fragmented Electronic Health Record (EHR) systems often takes
months or years.
2. The "Data-to-Knowledge" Bottleneck: Translating raw clinical data into
actionable, generalized science requires deep statistical analysis, peer
validation, and rigorous ethics reviews.
3. The "Knowledge-to-Performance" Bottleneck: Convincing busy clinicians to
change behavioral habits, altering software decision-support tools, and
shifting organizational culture requires massive effort.

Do you think the learning healthcare system framework sometimes takes too
much time per cycle to adapt to new discoveries?
Yes.
1. The "Performance-to-Data" Bottleneck: Aggregating clean, normalized data
across fragmented Electronic Health Record (EHR) systems often takes
months or years.
2. The "Data-to-Knowledge" Bottleneck: Translating raw clinical data into
actionable, generalized science requires deep statistical analysis, peer
validation, and rigorous ethics reviews.
3. The "Knowledge-to-Performance" Bottleneck: Convincing busy clinicians to
change behavioral habits, altering software decision-support tools, and
shifting organizational culture requires massive effort.
Fall 2025 Varatharajah, CSCI 5526 5

slideEntries.title: Student Questions
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Student Questions
We talked about data a lot today, and I heard from my friend who works in a
health insurance company that they are allowed to put PII/personal health
information in their LLM. Is this compliant with regulation, if so, how? Do they
just have to use "incognito mode" if using a 3rd party service? or do it on model
that is run on prem?
Health insurance companies handle PHI using two primary architectural paths
1. Enterprise Third-Party Cloud Models - if—and only if—the provider signs a
Business Associate Agreement (BAA) – a legally binding contract where the
AI vendor agrees to safeguard the health data under HIPAA standards.
2. On-Premises or Private Cloud Deployment

newborn populations.

Pediatric dosing guidelines were frequently calculated using a simple fraction of the

treatment and the new improved data is collected and used to retrain the model
how can we prevent bias?

lifecycle.

slideEntries.title: What is Classification?
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
What is Classification?
• Given an input X, assign it to class y.
• X can be a vector, image, text, etc.
• All possible classes (or values) of y should be known ahead of
time.
• Usually supervised: i.e., we have example pairs
((x 1 , y 1 ), ... . , (x N , y N ))
• Binary classification: y is one of two values (‘yes’ or ‘no’)
• Multiclass classification: y is one of multiple values
• Regression is an extension: y is in a continuous range

slideEntries.title: Generalization
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Generalization
• Components of generalization error
• Bias: how much the model differs from the true model?
• Error due to inaccurate assumptions/simplifications made by the model
• Variance: how much models estimated from different training sets differ from each
other
• Underfitting: model is too “simple” to represent all the relevant class
characteristics
• High bias and low variance
• High training error and high test error
• Overfitting: model is too “complex” and fits irrelevant characteristics
(noise) in the data
• Low bias and high variance
• Low training error and high test error
Slide credit: L. Lazebnik
Fall 2025 Varatharajah, CSCI 5526 24

slideEntries.title: PCA Steps
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
PCA Steps
• Given centered data X
• Rows are sensors and columns are measurements
• Each column contains the coordinates of each measurement with respect to
the original basis vectors (as defined by the sensors)
• Compute the covariance matrix (C X ) of X
• Perform eigenvalue decomposition of C X
• C X = E T DE (E contains the eigenvectors of C X in its rows)
• Define P = E
• Obtain new coordinates Y = PX
• Y are the coordinates of the measurements with respect to the new basis

slideEntries.explanation:

• Loadings = coefficients in eigenvectors of C X
• Help understand how original variables contribute to each of the PCs
• Positive loadings indicate that a variable and a principal component are
positively correlated: an increase in one results in an increase in the other.
• Negative loadings indicate a negative correlation.
• Large (either positive or negative) loadings indicate that a variable has a
strong effect on that principal component.
• Angles between vectors indicates correlation between them
• Loadings plot – plot of coefficients of original variables in each PC

slideEntries.title: Student Questions
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Student Questions
You mentioned using PCA on brain PET images in class. The three important
components explained only 9%, 8%, and 4% of the total variance in the data.
So, could PCA discard some low-variance features that carry the most clinical
information? How could we avoid this?
-- Yes, you must always inspect the components before throwing them away.
-- Sometimes you can have a criterion that is more clinically guided to
determine which components to keep.
What are the main limitations of using PCA within clinical data?
-- Linearity Assumption
-- Vulnerability to Outliers
-- Loss of Interpretability
-- Variance vs. Importance Mismatch

slideEntries.title: Student Questions
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Student Questions
How do we know the correct metrics for our use case? In healthcare what
metrics matter the most?
Recall / Sensitivity (True Positive Rate): This is often the top priority. Missing a
disease like cancer or sepsis (a false negative) can lead to severe harm or death.
Specificity (True Negative Rate): It matters when you want to avoid scaring healthy
patients or burdening clinics with unnecessary follow-up tests.
Precision (Positive Predictive Value): It is vital when a false positive triggers invasive
treatments, extreme anxiety, or a waste of limited hospital capacity.
AUPRC (Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve): In medicine, many conditions are
rare. AUPRC is more reliable than standard AUC-ROC for imbalanced datasets.
For imbalanced data, what methods can we use during model training to
improve sensitivity, even if it leads to a lower accuracy?
-- Adjust class weights in loss functions
-- Use sampling to increase minority samples or decrease majority samples
-- Use focal loss to prioritize harder minority samples
Fall 2026 Varatharajah, CSCI 5526 4

slideEntries.title: Hierarchical Clustering
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Hierarchical Clustering
• Works by creating a hierarchy based on similarity.
• Two different types:
• Agglomerative: Initially, each sample is in its own cluster. The
clusters are then merged step by step until a single cluster
remains.
• Divisive: Initially, all objects are in a single cluster. Then the division
process is performed step by step until each sample forms a
different cluster.
• Will describe agglomerative, more popular of the two.

easy to understand.

complexity.

their own disadvantages.

slideEntries.title: Determining the Number of
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Determining the Number of
Clusters
• Elbow method
• Use the turning point in the curve of sum of within cluster variance with
respect to the # of clusters (k).
• Cross validation method
• Divide a given data set into m parts.
• Use m-1 parts to obtain a clustering model.
• Use the remaining part to test the quality of the clustering.
• E.g., for each point in the test set, find the closest centroid, and use the sum of squared
distance between all points in the test set and the closest centroids to measure how well the
model fits the test set.
• Repeat it m times, compare the overall quality measure with respect to
different k’s, and find # of clusters that fits the data the best.

slideEntries.title: Extrinsic Methods
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Extrinsic Methods
• Clustering quality measure: Q(C, Cg), for a clustering C given the
ground truth Cg.
• Q is good if it satisfies the following criteria.
• Cluster homogeneity: A clustering result satisfies homogeneity if all of its
clusters contain data points which are members of a single class only.
• Cluster completeness: A clustering result satisfies completeness if all the
data points that are members of a given class are elements of the same
cluster.
• v-measure (beta is a weight specified in [0,1])
v = (1 + beta) * homogeneity * completeness / (beta * homogeneity + completeness)
Fall 2026 Varatharajah, CSCI 5526 38

slideEntries.explanation:

Intrinsic Measures: Silhouette Coefficient
• Silhouette Coefficient: a measure based on intra-cluster distances and
inter-cluster distances.
• For an individual point, i
• Calculate a = average distance of i to the points in its cluster
• Calculate b = min (average distance of i to points in another cluster)
• The silhouette coefficient for a point is then given by
s = b − a
b
• Typically, between 0 and 1.
• The closer to 1 the better.
• Can calculate the average Silhouette width for a cluster or all clusters. a

slideEntries.title: Student Questions
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Student Questions
Is it even worth always finding the most complicated way to map the (EHR)
data? Are simpler/cruder methods better?
Short answer is No!
Simpler methods are preferred because they can achieve 80-90% of the predictive
power with high interpretability and low overhead.
Complex mapping is potentially useful for:
• Rare Disease Research
• Long-horizon temporal deep learning
• Natural Language Processing of unstructured clinical notes
Is risk stratification growing due to the growth in deep learning? I'd imagine with
the data complexity and size it would help a lot, but how does the logistic
regression perform so well at the same time?
Yes, especially for applications based on unstructured data!
For many EHR-based ML tasks, logistic regression would work well for the above
reasons.
Fall 2026 Varatharajah, CSCI 5526 3

slideEntries.title: Student Questions
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Student Questions
In the second diabetes diagnosis scenario, how do we account for time-varying factors,
unobserved/latent variables that may arise during the gap between feature construction
and outcome determination? Are we assuming that the features constructed at baseline
adequately capture the patient’s future trajectory?
Yes, correct. Feature construction strategy is crucial and will determine the maximum
potential predictive capacity!
How can continuous physiological data, such as heart rate, be effectively represented and
encoded within an Electronic Health Record (EHR) system?
The EHR system typically does not encode continuous data streams, it only includes
compressed summary metrics.
Continuous data are typically stored in timeseries databases.

slideEntries.title: Potential Outcomes Framework
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Potential Outcomes Framework
(Rubin-Neyman Causal Model)
• Each unit (individual) x i has two potential outcomes:
• Y 0 (x i ) is the potential outcome had the unit not been treated:
“control outcome”
• Y 1 (x i ) is the potential outcome had the unit been treated:
“treated outcome”
• Conditional average treatment effect for unit i:
CATE x i = E (Y 1 − Y 0 )|x i = E Y 1 |x i ] − E[Y 0 |x i
• Average Treatment Effect:
ATE = E Y 1 − Y 0

slideEntries.title: Student Questions
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Student Questions
I'm not sure but what do you think to what extent causal inference can ever fully
replace randomized clinical trials?
Causal inference cannot replace RCTs ever. RCTs are still the gold-standard to
establish the efficacy of any intervention.
However, causal inference excels in some aspects:
1. When the interventions are harmful or happen over a long time
2. Typically, low cost because we use pre-existing data
3. High chance of generalizability since there are no strict
inclusion/exclusion criteria like in RCTs

slideEntries.title: Student Questions
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Student Questions
When using the parametric g-formula, how sensitive is the estimated ATE to the
choice or misspecification of the outcome model f(x,t), how does poor covariate
overlap between treated and control patients affect the estimate, how can we
assess whether the counterfactual predictions are reliable, and what can we do if
these assumptions appear to be violated?
1. It is highly sensitive to the choice of the model. For example, a high-bias
model could lead to errors that do not vanish with more data.
2. Poor covariate overlap also is problematic as it violates common support
assumption. The predictions can be artifactual and rely a lot on the
functional form of the model.
3. To ensure counterfactual predictions are reliable, you would do what you
do to evaluate a typical ML model fit. (look at training error, test error,
etc).
Fall 2026 Varatharajah, CSCI 5526 5

treatment arms.

Convolutions as Universal Feature Extractors
• An array operation where each output data element is a
weighted sum of a collection of neighboring input elements
• The weights used in the weighted sum calculation are
defined by an input mask array, commonly referred to as
the convolution kernel
• Sometimes referred to as convolution masks or convolution filters.
• The same kernel is typically used for all elements of the array.

slideEntries.title: ECG Classification
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
ECG Classification
• 30s windows as input (sampled at 200Hz)
• 16 residual blocks with 2 conv layers per block.
• The conv layers all have a filter length of 16 and
have 64k filters, where k starts out as 1 and is
incremented every 4-th residual block.
• Every alternate residual block subsamples its
inputs by a factor of 2 (i.e., max pool).
• When a residual block subsamples the input, the
corresponding shortcut connections also
subsample their input using a max pooling
operation with the same subsample factor.
Fall 2026 Varatharajah, CSCI 5526 46
Source: Nature
Hannun, A.Y., Rajpurkar, P., Haghpanahi, M. et al. Cardiologist-level arrhythmia detection and classification in
ambulatory electrocardiograms using a deep neural network. Nat Med

slideEntries.title: Student Questions
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Student Questions
How does the MaxPooling layer in a Convolutional Neural Network help
preserve important features, such as tumors or lesions, while reducing the
dimensionality of medical images? What are the potential risks of losing critical
diagnostic information during pooling?
Max-pooling will preserve high-contrast/sharp features. Tumors and lesions
often manifest as high-contrast regions or sharp intensity spikes w.r.t. the
background. These will have high activation values in a CNN and will pass
through max-pool layers.
However, there is a significant risk if the important features have
heterogeneous shapes/attributes.
Fall 2026 Varatharajah, CSCI 5526 3

slideEntries.title: Student Questions
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Student Questions
Which padding method is used most often in medical imaging models?
Same padding (aka zero padding) is most common as it preserves the
dimensions.
For temporal medical data, do people use RNNs or LSTMs? Or even hybrid
model like Conv-LSTMs?
Yes, if there is a need to learn morphological patterns before the temporal
patterns (such as in signal data), adding conv layers before RNN/LSTM layers
is useful.

we aren’t sure yet?

models.
If you want to experiment with a custom architecture, then it is OK to keep
the description a bit general.
But please do think about the input size, dataset size, and other relevant
aspects to narrow down the architectural choice.

slideEntries.title: Student Questions
slideEntries.explanation:
Computer Science & Engineering Computer Science & Engineering
Student Questions
How do you determine # of convolution layers and/or dimensions to reduce to in
each layer?
If you have a large dataset:
classification: 5-10 convolutional layers
segmentation: 10-20 convolutional layers with skip connections
For a small dataset: 3-5 convolutional layers to reduce overfitting risk
Generally, reduce spatial dimensions progressively (e.g., halving at each step),
while doubling feature channels to capture more abstract representations.
For segmentation tasks, if you downsample too much and you lose fine
boundary details.
For classification, it’s okay to reduce more aggressively as long as you preserve
semantic meaning.

slideEntries.explanation:

Student Questions
How to choose appropriate architecture for the dataset we have? Are there any
key considerations?
Dataset size:
>10k images: train a deep model from scratch
1k-10k images: pretrained model + finetuning
<1k images: transfer learning or custom architectures
For Segmentation
• U-Net: Efficient for small datasets, captures fine features.
• nnU-Net: Auto-adapts architecture to your dataset. Strong default.
• Attention U-Net: Highlights relevant features (good for small/ambiguous
lesions).
For Classification
• ResNet-18/34: Simple, low risk of overfitting.
• DenseNet: Good at feature reuse, often better for small datasets.
• EfficientNet: Highly optimized, but sensitive to training settings.
